entities.summary:
Domingo Fernández Navarrete (1618–1689) was a Spanish Dominican friar, missionary, and later Archbishop of Santo Domingo, whose extensive travels and writings provided one of the most detailed and critical European accounts of 17th-century China. A pivotal figure in the contentious Chinese Rites Controversy, Navarrete became a staunch opponent of the Jesuit accommodationist approach, advocating for a stricter interpretation of Catholic doctrine regarding local customs. His life trajectory, spanning from the Iberian Peninsula to the distant reaches of East Asia and the Caribbean, exemplifies the globalized reach of the Spanish Empire and the fervent evangelistic zeal of the Early Modern era.

After joining the Dominicans in 1635, Navarrete embarked on his missionary journey to the Philippines in 1646, where he taught theology at the University of Santo Tomas in Manila. In 1658, he ventured into China, establishing missions in Fujian province. However, the escalating persecution of Christians led to his arrest and eventual expulsion in 1669, alongside other missionaries. His subsequent return to Europe saw him actively engage with the Sacred Congregation de Propaganda Fide in Rome, pressing his arguments against the Jesuit methods and contributing significantly to the theological debates that would shape future missionary policy. He was appointed Archbishop of Santo Domingo in 1677, serving until his death.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Domingo Fernández Navarrete's detailed writings provided invaluable, albeit controversial, European insights into 17th-century China and profoundly influenced the Vatican's condemnation of the Chinese Rites, shaping Catholic missionary policy for centuries. His work remains a primary source for understanding early modern East-West cultural and religious encounters.
